To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) V(A)/Q impairment is present in all stages of COPD, (ii) V(A)/q impairment is disproportionately greater than FEV(1), and (iii) the degree of hypoxemia and hypercapnia is modestly greater in patients with greater airflow limitation.
ventilation-perfusion imbalance and hypoxemia increase in proportion to airflow limitation across the spectrum of COPD severity.

ventilation-perfusion imbalance, predominantly perfusional, is disproportionately greater to airflow limitation in COPD stage 1, and increases with COPD progression, but is modestly related to spirometric severity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between airflow limitation and gas exchange in COPD, and the role of ventilation/perfusion (V(A)Q) inequality in the pathophysiology and clinical course of the disease.
the relationship of ventilation-perfusion imbalance to chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD).

the pathogenesis of COPD, the relationship between gas exchange and spirometric abnormalities in COPD, the role of pulmonary gas exchange abnormalities in the development of pulmonary hypertension and right heart dysfunction in COPD, and the role of gas exchange abnormalities in determining the response of COPD to bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen, and pulmonary rehabilitation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between ventilation and perfusion in COPD is not as simple as one would expect from a disease that is primarily a problem of airflow limitation.

the severity of COPD is determined by the severity of the airflow limitation, but that the severity of the V/A/Q mismatch and hypoxaemia is also determined by the severity and distribution of the airflow limitation.
the relationship between pulmonary function and gas exchange in COPD depends on the severity of the disease and the method of assessment of gas exchange.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
V(A)/Q inequalities in COPD are more pronounced than airflow limitation in mild disease and that the progression of both abnormalities is modest with disease severity.
ventilation-perfusion imbalance is a key feature of COPD, and its relationship with airflow limitation is complex and not well understood.
V(A)/Q impairment is present early in the course of COPD and increases only modestly as airflow limitation worsens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ventilation-perfusion imbalance and arterial oxygenation are more closely related to FEV1 than to the severity of COPD.
ventilation-perfusion imbalance and hypoxemia increase across the severity spectrum of COPD, but the relationship is not linear.

V(A)/Q inequalities are disproportionately large relative to airflow limitation in early COPD, and this may reflect pathogenic mechanisms that reduce local ventilation and blood perfusion in the same regions.
